lead: The CMOS inverter is one nMOS pull-down and one pMOS pull-up with their gates tied together. Its voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) plots the output V<sub>out</sub> against the input V<sub>in</sub> at a fixed supply V<sub>DD</sub>. From this one curve come the switching threshold V<sub>M</sub>, the output levels V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub>, the input limits V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub>, and the two noise margins. They tell a designer how much noise an input can take, so the VTC is the first check on every standard cell.
prereq: You need: the square-law drain current of the MOSFET in its cut-off, linear and saturation regions (see MOSFET I-V characteristics and device equations).

sections.h3: The five regions of the VTC

blocks.text: The nMOS source is at ground, so its V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>; the pMOS source is at V<sub>DD</sub>, so its V<sub>SG</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>in</sub>. No current leaves the output, so the two drain currents are equal, and each region of the curve is the pair of transistor states that satisfies this.

Saturation: I<sub>D</sub> = (k/2)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>t</sub>)². Linear: I<sub>D</sub> = k[(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>t</sub>)V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2]. Here k = µC<sub>ox</sub>(W/L) is the device gain in A/V² (some books write β).

At V<sub>M</sub> both devices are saturated. Setting k<sub>n</sub>(V<sub>M</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>)² = k<sub>p</sub>(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>M</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)² and taking square roots gives the design equation:
VM = (VDD + rVtn − |Vtp|)/(1 + r) Here r = √(kn/kp) is the strength ratio. A stronger nMOS (r > 1) pulls VM below VDD/2; a stronger pMOS pushes it up.

V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> are the flat output levels: V<sub>DD</sub> and 0 V for a static CMOS inverter, because one transistor is always off. V<sub>IL</sub> is the largest input that still counts as a 0 and V<sub>IH</sub> the smallest that still counts as a 1. Both are taken where the slope dV<sub>out</sub>/dV<sub>in</sub> = −1; between them the gate amplifies noise instead of rejecting it.
NMH = VOH − VIH, NML = VIL − VOL Here nMH and NML are the high and low noise margins in volts: how far a valid output can be pushed by noise before the next gate misreads it.

For a matched inverter (k<sub>n</sub> = k<sub>p</sub> and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = V<sub>t</sub>) the slope condition can be solved in closed form. In region B the nMOS is saturated and the pMOS linear; differentiating the current equality and putting the slope at −1 gives:
VIL = (3VDD + 2Vt)/8, VIH = (5VDD − 2Vt)/8 Here both margins then equal (3VDD + 2Vt)/8, and VM = VDD/2.

Electrons are about two to three times more mobile than holes, so equal widths do not give a matched pair. To centre V<sub>M</sub>, the pMOS is made wider by the mobility ratio: W<sub>p</sub>/W<sub>n</sub> = µ<sub>n</sub>/µ<sub>p</sub>. When V<sub>M</sub> moves away from V<sub>DD</sub>/2, one margin grows and the other shrinks, and the smaller one sets the noise budget.
In region C the gain is much larger than 1, so a slightly bad input comes out as a clean rail. This regeneration is why long chains of CMOS gates do not lose their levels.

Some syllabi call the VTC the DC transfer characteristic; the two VTCs of an SRAM cell drawn on one graph form the butterfly curve. The inverter's widths also set its load and delay (see switching characteristics).

examples.question: A matched CMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V, with k<sub>n</sub> = k<sub>p</sub>. Find V<sub>M</sub>, V<sub>IL</sub>, V<sub>IH</sub> and both noise margins, and check the transistor regions at V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>M</sub>.
steps: Matched means r = 1, so V<sub>M</sub> = (3.3 + 0.6 − 0.6)/2 = 1.65 V.

At V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>out</sub> = 1.65 V the nMOS has V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>t</sub> = 1.05 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.65 V > 1.05 V, so it is saturated. The pMOS has V<sub>SG</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 1.65 − 0.6 = 1.05 V and V<sub>SD</sub> = 1.65 V > 1.05 V, so it is saturated too.
V<sub>OH</sub> = 3.3 V and V<sub>OL</sub> = 0 V, so NM<sub>L</sub> = 1.39 − 0 = 1.39 V and NM<sub>H</sub> = 3.3 − 1.91 = 1.39 V.
Check on the computed curve (Figure 3.1.1): the slope is −1 at both points, where the output is 3.04 V and 0.26 V.
examples.answer: V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V with both devices saturated; V<sub>IL</sub> ≈ 1.39 V, V<sub>IH</sub> ≈ 1.91 V; NM<sub>L</sub> = NM<sub>H</sub> ≈ 1.39 V.

examples.question: The same process has µ<sub>n</sub> = 2.5µ<sub>p</sub>. A designer draws the pMOS with the same W/L as the nMOS. Find V<sub>M</sub> at V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V. What W<sub>p</sub>/W<sub>n</sub> would bring V<sub>M</sub> back to 1.65 V?
steps: Equal sizes give k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub> = µ<sub>n</sub>/µ<sub>p</sub> = 2.5, so r = √2.5 = 1.581.
V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V needs r = 1, that is k<sub>p</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>, so µ<sub>p</sub>W<sub>p</sub> = µ<sub>n</sub>W<sub>n</sub> and W<sub>p</sub>/W<sub>n</sub> = 2.5.
examples.answer: V<sub>M</sub> ≈ 1.41 V, 0.24 V below the centre, so NM<sub>L</sub> shrinks; a pMOS 2.5 times wider restores V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V.

traps: Writing V<sub>M</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>/2 for every inverter. It holds only when k<sub>n</sub> = k<sub>p</sub> and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>|; with equal widths the stronger nMOS pulls V<sub>M</sub> down.
Writing the pMOS overdrive as V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|. Its source sits at V<sub>DD</sub>, so the overdrive is V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|.
Taking V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub> as the thresholds V<sub>tn</sub> and V<sub>DD</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|. They are the points where the slope is −1, inside regions B and D.

Swapping the margin formulas. NM<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub> and NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>; logic swing V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> is a different, larger number.

quiz.q: Define V<sub>M</sub>, V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> for a CMOS inverter.
quiz.a: V<sub>M</sub> is the input voltage at which V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>. V<sub>OH</sub> is the output level for a low input and V<sub>OL</sub> the output level for a high input; for static CMOS they are V<sub>DD</sub> and 0 V.

quiz.q: Why does an ideal CMOS inverter draw no current from V<sub>DD</sub> when its input is held at 0 V or V<sub>DD</sub>?
quiz.a: At either rail one transistor is off, so there is no conducting path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground. The transistor that is on connects the output to its own rail and carries current only while it charges or discharges the load.

quiz.q: An inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V and k<sub>n</sub> = 4k<sub>p</sub>. Find V<sub>M</sub>.
A matched inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V and V<sub>t</sub> = 0.5 V. Find V<sub>IL</sub>, V<sub>IH</sub> and the noise margins.
A designer doubles k<sub>n</sub> in a matched inverter. How do V<sub>M</sub> and the two noise margins move?
quiz.a: r becomes √2 = 1.41, so V<sub>M</sub> drops below V<sub>DD</sub>/2. The whole curve shifts left: V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub> both fall, so NM<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub> grows and NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> shrinks. The smaller margin, NM<sub>L</sub>, now limits the gate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cell libraries are released only after the VTC is simulated at every process, voltage and temperature corner. For SRAM, the largest square that fits inside the lobes of the butterfly curve is the static noise margin. Search next for static noise margin, SPICE DC sweep and process corners.

figure.caption: The computed transfer curve of the matched 3.3 V inverter: the slope is −1 at V<sub>IL</sub> = 1.39 V and V<sub>IH</sub> = 1.91 V, and the curve crosses V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> at V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V. With equal widths (dashed) the stronger nMOS pulls V<sub>M</sub> down to 1.41 V.

spec.aria: Plot of output voltage against input voltage for a 3.3 volt CMOS inverter. The solid matched curve crosses the diagonal at 1.65 volts and has slope minus one at 1.39 and 1.91 volts; a dashed curve for equal widths crosses at 1.41 volts.
